_comment: Rules that read the code rather than the text of it. Each carries one tree-sitter query per language, so teaching a rule about another language is an entry here rather than a change in Rust. What a query cannot express is judgment — whether the argument is a literal, which decides between an ugly call and a dangerous one — and that lives in ast.rs where it can be tested. Captures: @hit is what gets reported, @arg is the argument judged for literalness.

rules.title: Code is built at run time and executed
rules.description: A value decided while the app is running is handed to something that executes it as code.
rules.impact: If any part of that value can be influenced from outside, whoever influences it chooses what the app does next.
rules.fix: Work out what the code is actually for. A lookup table, a match on a fixed set of names, or a small parser will do the job without running text as code.

safeArgumentPatterns.shell: ^"?\$\((ssh-agent|brew shellenv|pyenv init|rbenv init|nodenv init|direnv hook|opam env|conda shell)[^$`]*\)"?$

rules.title: A shell command is built from a value
rules.description: A command line is assembled from something other than fixed text and handed to the shell.
rules.impact: A semicolon or a backtick in the wrong place turns one command into two, and the second one is whatever the attacker wanted.
rules.fix: Pass the program and its arguments as a list instead of a string, so the shell never parses them. Where a shell is genuinely needed, validate the value against a fixed set first.

rules.title: A database query is built by joining text together
rules.description: A query is assembled from pieces rather than sent with its values kept separate.
rules.impact: A quote in someone's name is enough to change what the query does, and a deliberate one can read or delete any table the app can reach.
rules.fix: Send the query with placeholders and pass the values alongside it. Every database library supports this, and it is shorter than building the string.

rules.title: Data from outside is turned back into objects unsafely
rules.description: A format that can describe arbitrary objects is being read with the reader that builds them.
rules.impact: Reading the data is enough to run code: the attacker does not need the app to use the result, only to load it.
rules.fix: Use the safe reader — yaml.safe_load rather than yaml.load — and prefer a format that carries data only, such as JSON, for anything that arrives from outside.

rules.title: A command is run with backticks, built from text
rules.description: Backticks run a shell command and hand back its output. This one is assembled from pieces rather than written out.
rules.impact: Whatever ends up inside the backticks is run by a shell, so a semicolon in someone's input starts a second command with the app's own permissions.
rules.fix: Run the program directly with its arguments as a list, rather than building one string for a shell to pull apart.

rules.title: A command built from text is run through a shell it was asked for
rules.description: The program is told to hand this command to a shell (`shell=True` in Python, `shell: true` in Node.js, `runInShell: true` in Dart), and the command or its arguments are assembled from pieces rather than written out.
rules.impact: Whatever ends up in the command is run by a shell, so a semicolon or a quote in someone's input starts a second command with the app's own permissions.
rules.fix: Leave the shell option out and pass the program and its arguments separately, as in Python's subprocess.run(["notes-export", title, "out.pdf"]) or Node's execFile("notes-export", [title, "out.pdf"]). Each argument then reaches the program as it is, and nothing in it is read as shell syntax.

rules.title: A file is opened at a path built from a value
rules.description: A file path used to read, write or delete a file is built from a value rather than written out, so the file operation goes wherever that value points.
rules.impact: If any part of the path comes from a request, a name like ../../etc/passwd reads or overwrites a file outside the folder the app meant to use.
rules.fix: Keep user-submitted file names out of file paths: store files under names the app generates, and look them up by id. Where a submitted name has to be used, reduce it to a bare name (secure_filename in Flask, path.basename in Node) and check that the resolved path is still inside the folder it should be in.

rules.title: A disallowed hash function is used
rules.description: MD5 or SHA-1 is used as a hash function. Both have practical collision attacks, and approved-hash rules disallow them for any cryptographic use.
rules.impact: Anything that relies on the hash to tell two things apart, or to prove something was not changed, can be fooled by somebody who builds a second input with the same hash. Used for passwords, both are also fast enough to guess through quickly.
rules.fix: Use SHA-256 or stronger for integrity and signatures, and a password hashing function (Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt) for passwords. If this hash is only a cache key or a file checksum with no security purpose, say so where it is used; Python lets you pass usedforsecurity=False.

rules.title: A cipher or block mode that is not approved is used
rules.description: Data is encrypted with ECB, the block mode that encrypts equal blocks to equal output, or with a retired cipher such as DES, triple DES, RC4, RC2 or Blowfish.
rules.impact: ECB leaves the shape of the data visible through the encryption, and the retired ciphers can be broken or have known practical attacks, so the encrypted data is less private than it looks.
rules.fix: Use AES with GCM (or ChaCha20-Poly1305) through your language's high-level library, which chooses the mode and the nonce for you. In Java, always name the mode: Cipher.getInstance("AES") quietly means ECB.
rules.looksFor: encryption in ECB mode, or with a retired cipher such as DES, triple DES, RC4, RC2, or Blowfish

looksForIn.shell: openssl asked to encrypt with one of those ciphers or modes

rules.title: Data is encrypted in a way that does not show whether it was changed
rules.description: Data is encrypted with a block mode that keeps it secret but cannot tell when it has been altered: CBC, CTR, CFB, or OFB. Someone who can change the encrypted data can often change what it decrypts to, without knowing the key.
rules.impact: Encrypted data that is stored or sent somewhere a person can reach, such as a cookie, a token, or a file, can be tampered with, and the app will decrypt and trust the altered result. With CBC, error messages about padding can also let somebody decrypt it bit by bit.
rules.fix: Use an authenticated mode: AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, or a library that does it for you (Fernet, libsodium's secretbox, Tink). If this code already signs the encrypted data with a separate HMAC and checks it before decrypting, it is correct as it is: this rule sees one call at a time and cannot see the HMAC, which is why it is only ever a finding and never a clean result.
rules.looksFor: encryption in CBC, CTR, CFB, or OFB mode, which keeps data secret but does not show whether it was changed; only ever a finding, because a separate HMAC elsewhere can make it correct

looksForIn.shell: openssl asked to encrypt with one of those modes

rules.title: The app redirects to a destination built from a value
rules.description: A redirect sends the user to a destination that is built from a value rather than written out or produced from the app's own routes.
rules.impact: If the destination comes from the request, as a ?next= parameter usually does, a link on the app's own domain can send somebody to a lookalike sign-in page on another domain, and the address they clicked was genuine.
rules.fix: Redirect only to the app's own routes, built with its router (url_for, reverse, a Rails _path helper), or check the destination against a short list of allowed hosts. For a return-to address, accept only a path that starts with a single / and not //.

rules.title: Code downloaded from the network is run straight away
rules.description: A script downloads a third-party component and hands it to a shell or an interpreter as it arrives, so it runs whatever the address serves, with nothing checking it came from the expected repository or is the version meant.
rules.impact: Whoever controls that address, or anything between it and the machine, chooses what runs, with the permissions of the script, often root.
rules.fix: Download to a file, check it against a published checksum or signature, then run it. Better still, install the tool from the system's package manager, or pin a version in a lockfile.

rules.title: A WebSocket address without encryption is written into the code
rules.description: A `ws://` address to another computer is written into the code. `ws://` is a WebSocket with no encryption, the way `http://` is a page without it.
rules.impact: Everything sent over the connection, including the session it was opened with and whatever the person types, can be read and changed by anybody on the network between them and the app: the same café Wi-Fi, a compromised router.
rules.fix: Use `wss://`. In a browser, build the address from the page's own, so it follows the page to HTTPS: `(location.protocol === 'https:' ? 'wss://' : 'ws://') + location.host + '/socket'`.
rules.looksFor: a `ws://` address to another computer written into the code

looksForIn.shell: a `ws://` address to another computer given to a command, quoted or not

rules.title: A signature is compared in a way that leaks how much of it was right
rules.description: A keyed signature (an HMAC, the kind a webhook or a signed link carries) is checked with an ordinary equals comparison. An ordinary comparison stops at the first character that differs, so it is not constant-time: it takes slightly longer the more of the signature is right.
rules.impact: Someone who can send many guesses and time the answers can work out a valid signature one character at a time, and then forge the requests the signature was meant to prove came from you or your partner.
rules.fix: Compare with the constant-time function your language provides: `hmac.compare_digest` in Python, `crypto.timingSafeEqual` in Node.js (on two buffers of the same length), `hash_equals` in PHP, `Rack::Utils.secure_compare` in Ruby, `hmac.Equal` in Go, `MessageDigest.isEqual` in Java and Kotlin, `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals` in C#, the `hmac` crate's `verify_slice` in Rust, `CRYPTO_memcmp` or `sodium_memcmp` in C and C++, and `HMAC.isValidAuthenticationCode` in Swift.

rules.title: A model file is loaded in a way that can run code
rules.description: A model is loaded with a reader that can run code while it loads: joblib (which is pickle underneath), `torch.load` with `weights_only=False`, `torch.hub.load`, NumPy with `allow_pickle=True`, Keras with `safe_mode=False`, or a Hugging Face model with `trust_remote_code=True` or `use_safetensors=False`.
rules.impact: Whoever can change the model file, or the model repository it is downloaded from, can make it run any code they like on your server the moment the app loads it.
rules.fix: Load models only in formats that hold numbers and no code: safetensors, GGUF, or ONNX. For PyTorch, keep `weights_only=True` (the default since PyTorch 2.6). Leave `trust_remote_code` off unless you have read the code and pinned the revision it comes from.
rules.looksFor: Python model loading that can run code: `joblib.load`, `torch.hub.load`, and the settings that turn a safe loader unsafe (`weights_only=False`, `allow_pickle=True`, `safe_mode=False`, `trust_remote_code=True`, `use_safetensors=False`); `pickle.load` itself is the unsafe-deserialization rule's, and model files committed to the folder are not opened, so finding none credits nothing

rules.title: A model is downloaded by name without pinning the exact version
rules.description: The app downloads a model from Hugging Face by its name (`organization/model`) without a `revision` set to a commit hash. By name alone, it gets whatever the model's owner uploaded last, with nothing to check it against.
rules.impact: If the model repository is changed, by its owner or by someone who took it over, the app starts using the new model on its next download with nobody having looked at it. The model you tested is then not the model you run, and nothing can prove which one you have.
rules.fix: Add `revision="<40-character commit hash>"` to the call, taken from the model's page on Hugging Face (Files and versions, then the commit), and change it on purpose when you upgrade.
rules.looksFor: a Hugging Face model named in the code as `organization/model` and downloaded without `revision` set to a commit hash; a name built at run time, and downloads done outside the code (a script, `ollama pull`, a model server image), are not seen, so finding none credits nothing

rules.title: A hosted model is asked for by a name that moves
rules.description: The code asks the AI provider for a model by a name ending in `-latest` (or `:latest`). The provider points that name at a new model whenever it releases one.
rules.impact: The model behind the app can change on the provider's schedule with no change to your code, so nothing prompts anyone to test the new one for safety before users meet it.
rules.fix: Name a dated model version (for example `gpt-4o-2024-08-06` rather than `chatgpt-4o-latest`), and when you move to a new one, do it on purpose and re-run your checks.
rules.looksFor: a model name ending in `-latest` or `:latest` written into the code as text, for the common provider families (Claude, GPT, Gemini, Mistral, Llama, and others); a name read from settings or an environment variable is not seen, so finding none credits nothing

looksForIn.shell: a model name ending in `-latest` or `:latest` given to a command, such as `ollama run llama3:latest`, quoted or not

rules.title: A key is made from a password with too few rounds of work
rules.description: A key is derived from a password with PBKDF2, and the number of rounds written into the code is below 210,000, the lowest figure OWASP recommends for any PBKDF2 hash (210,000 for SHA-512; SHA-256 needs 600,000 and SHA-1 1,300,000).
rules.impact: Anyone who gets hold of what the key protects, such as an encrypted backup, an export, or a stored hash, can try guesses at the password quickly on ordinary hardware, and most people's passwords fall to a fast guesser.
rules.fix: Raise the number of rounds to at least 600,000 for PBKDF2 with SHA-256 (210,000 with SHA-512), or use a password hashing function made for this, such as Argon2id or scrypt. Keep the count where it can be raised later without breaking what was already stored.

rules.title: The app serves files from the folder its own code is in
rules.description: A static-file handler is given the folder the code itself is in, or the folder the app was started from, rather than a folder that holds only files meant for visitors.
rules.impact: Everything beside the code can be downloaded by anyone who guesses its name: the source code, the settings, a `.env` file with keys in it, a database file, and backups. That shows how the app works and often hands over its secrets.
rules.fix: Keep the files visitors should get (pages, images, styles, scripts for the browser) in a folder of their own, such as `public` or `static`, and point the handler only at that folder.

rules.title: A token check is told not to check who the token is for
rules.description: The code checks a signed token (such as a JWT) with its audience check switched off: `verify_aud` set to false in PyJWT, python-jose, or ruby-jwt; `ValidateAudience = false` in .NET; `validate_aud = false` in Rust's `jsonwebtoken`; `SkipClientIDCheck: true` in Go's `go-oidc`; or `WithoutClaimsValidation()` in Go's `golang-jwt`, which skips the audience with every other claim.
rules.impact: A token made for a different app or service, signed by the same sign-in server, is accepted here as if it were meant for this app. Somebody who holds a token for any service that server signs for can use it to get in.
rules.fix: Turn the audience check back on and give it this app's own name, the one the sign-in server writes into the token's `aud` field (for example `audience="my-api"` in PyJWT, `ValidAudience` in .NET, `set_audience` in Rust, or the client ID in `go-oidc`). In .NET, an `AudienceValidator` of your own still runs when `ValidateAudience` is false; if you wrote one on purpose, say so to whoever reads this finding.
rules.looksFor: the explicit switches that turn a token's audience check off: `verify_aud` false (Python, Ruby), `ValidateAudience = false` (C#), `validate_aud = false` (Rust), `SkipClientIDCheck: true` and `WithoutClaimsValidation()` (Go); a check that is simply never given an audience is not looked for, so finding none credits nothing

rules.title: A sign-in token is allowed to say where the key that checks it comes from
rules.description: The code reads, from a signed token (such as a JWT) it has not yet checked, where its key is to come from: the `jku` header (the address of a set of keys), `x5u` (the address of a certificate), or `jwk` (the key itself), and hands that straight to something that fetches a key or makes one. The token is choosing the key it will be checked with.
rules.impact: Anybody can make a key of their own, sign a token saying they are any user or an admin, and point the token at their own key: the app fetches it, the signature checks out, and they are in. A `jku` or `x5u` address also makes the app fetch whatever address an outsider writes.
rules.fix: Take keys only from your sign-in server's own address, written in your settings, never from the token: for example `PyJWKClient(JWKS_URL)` in Python, `createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(JWKS_URL))` with `jose` or `jwksClient({ jwksUri: JWKS_URL })` in Node.js, and choose the key from that set by the token's `kid`. Ignore `jku`, `x5u`, and `jwk` in the token. If the app must follow them, compare the whole address with a fixed list of your sign-in server's addresses before fetching anything; if this line already comes after such a check, the finding is wrong, and `sv review` can record that.
